text:
Nigeria’s oil fortunes have surged amid global disruptions triggered by the United States/Israel war on Iran, which sent crude prices soaring above the conservative benchmark of $64.85 per barrel set in the 2026 budget. With Brent crude averaging nearly $97 per barrel over six months, the country has earned billions of dollars in additional revenue, estimated at N4.78 trillion above projections.
Yet the government has offered no transparent account of how this windfall is being managed. The opacity is striking: while allocations to states have risen modestly, the Excess Crude Account remains at a paltry $535,823, and no clear policy has been announced to cushion citizens against the cost-of-living crisis.
According to a Daily Trust report published on October 6, 2026, Nigeria’s daily oil production averaged 1.57 million barrels. Although below the OPEC quota, this output still generated significant returns because of the sharp rise in international crude prices. Since President Bola Ahmed Tinubu removed the fuel subsidy in 2023, Nigerians have been forced to pay exorbitant prices at the pump, with petrol now costing more than nine times its price under the subsidy regime.
At the same time, the naira was devalued, ending the long-standing argument that the government was subsidising the currency against the US dollar. Higher taxes have further burdened households and businesses. These measures have boosted government revenues, reflected in rising monthly allocations to the federal, state and local governments. With so much money flowing into public coffers, the administration cannot credibly argue that it lacks resources or that the oil windfall is insignificant.
While the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) announced that foreign reserves had risen to $55.08 billion as of October 9, 2026, one of their highest levels in nearly two decades, it made no reference to the extraordinary oil receipts generated since February, when global crude prices spiked following the war. This omission is troubling. The government has provided no clear account of how the additional revenue has been spent. There is no evidence that the National Assembly has debated the surplus revenue or that a supplementary budget has been presented to authorise its expenditure. The failure to explain the relationship between rising reserves and the oil windfall raises serious questions about transparency.
More troubling is that, rather than transparently deploying the windfall to ease hardship and reduce borrowing, the government continues to accumulate debt. Nigeria’s debt to the World Bank stands at $20.73 billion, making it the institution’s largest borrower in Africa and third-largest globally. In June 2026, the country’s exposure to the International Development Association (IDA) rose to $19.12 billion, while another $1.61 billion was owed to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD). The government has also sought fresh loans worth $1.75 billion, including $1.25 billion for energy access and broadband connectivity and $500 million for agricultural value chains under the AGROW project. The World Bank has warned that Nigeria’s growing external debt could undermine long-term economic stability.
The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has created a sharp divide among oil-producing nations. Iraq and Qatar, whose exports depend heavily on the strategic waterway, have struggled to move their crude oil and gas, suffering revenue shortfalls despite soaring global prices. Iraq faces the challenge of repairing damaged infrastructure and paying public salaries, while Qatar has had to draw on its sovereign wealth fund to maintain liquidity. Nigeria, however, is not directly affected by the blockade. Its exports bypass Hormuz, allowing it to benefit from the price surge triggered by the US–Iran war. This gives the country a rare opportunity to earn additional revenue while others face shortfalls.
Other nations have seized the opportunity to strengthen their economies. Norway has channelled oil revenues into its Government Pension Fund Global, the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, to safeguard long-term prosperity. Saudi Arabia has used its East-West Pipeline to bypass Hormuz, while pursuing its Vision 2030 programme to diversify the economy through projects such as NEOM and investments in tourism, sports and technology. The United Arab Emirates has also rerouted exports through Fujairah, helping it maintain supplies and economic activity despite disruptions.
Nigeria’s position is striking. Like Norway and Saudi Arabia, it has benefited from oil exports and higher prices. Yet, unlike these countries, it has failed to articulate a clear plan for managing the windfall. There is no publicly established framework for its use or evidence of legislative debate on how the surplus will be spent. This lack of transparency is indefensible. Nigerians are enduring inflation, high fuel costs and rising taxes, while billions in additional oil receipts remain unaccounted for. At a time of global crisis, silence is not strategy; it is failure.
We insist that the government accounts for the additional revenue generated from crude oil sales at higher prices. The windfall should be strategically deployed to ease the economic burden on citizens and strengthen the country’s fiscal buffers. A significant portion should go towards rebuilding the Excess Crude Account, which has dwindled to near insignificance, to help the nation withstand future shocks without plunging into crisis. Some of the funds should be invested in critical infrastructure, including power, transport and healthcare, to improve productivity and living standards. The government should also use part of the windfall to support exchange-rate stability, ease inflationary pressures and provide targeted relief to households struggling with high fuel and food costs.
Transparency is paramount. Nigerians must know how much has been earned, where the money is held and precisely how it will be spent. Silence is not an option. The government must publish a clear account of the windfall and its proposed allocation. Only through openness and accountability can this rare opportunity be transformed into lasting benefits for the people.
